passage: I'm Gurleen, Anand's didi, and I saw the whole thing. Mummy's office friends came for lunch on Sunday. Before they arrived she told Anand, nine: sit straight, no running, no talking with food in your mouth, guests eat first. Anand nodded like a soldier. He passed the chole, said 'Thank you, Aunty,' and even laughed at their boring jokes. But when the gulab jamuns came out, the guests took four each and the bowl came back empty. Anand's face went very still. He said nothing. The minute the door closed, he flopped on the sofa, kicked off his socks and shouted, 'Finally! Now can I be normal?' I think he was only half joking.

qa.q: What happened to the gulab jamun bowl?
qa.a: The bowl came back empty.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when the gulab jamun bowl came back empty?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and resentful, though he kept his face still and said nothing in front of the guests.

qa.q: What could Mummy do next time to make guest days feel fairer to Anand?
qa.a: Set aside a few gulab jamuns for him beforehand and thank him afterwards for his effort, so good manners don't cost him his favourite sweet.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see Anand's shout of 'Now can I be normal?'
qa.a: Gurleen thinks it was only half a joke, reading it as a real sign that being on show for the guests was tiring for him.

grounding: Shows a child told to sit properly, stay quiet and let guests eat first, who misses a favourite sweet and feels the gap between the home's public and private faces.

passage:
Thursday: Mumma lays out the rules for Saturday's dinner with Papa's new boss. 'Sit properly, speak only when asked, and guests eat first.' Trisha, ten, rolls her eyes but nods.
Saturday: Trisha sits straight in her ironed frock for two hours. The paneer tikka she helped marinate goes round the guests twice and is finished before it reaches her. She smiles, says, 'No, thank you, I'm full,' and her stomach growls.
Monday: At recess Trisha tells her friend Disha, 'At home we have two faces. One for guests and one for us.' Disha laughs. 'Same. Our real face eats standing up in the kitchen.'

qa.q: Which dish did Trisha help marinate?
qa.a: The paneer tikka.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when she said, 'No, thank you, I'm full'?
qa.a: She felt hungry and quietly resentful, hiding her disappointment behind a polite smile while her stomach growled.

qa.q: What could Mumma do so Trisha doesn't miss the dish she helped make?
qa.a: Keep a small portion aside for Trisha before serving, and let her mention that she helped make it, so she feels included.

qa.q: What does Disha's reply suggest about how Disha sees guest days?
qa.a: Disha recognises the same two faces at home, polite for guests and relaxed in private, and treats it with humour.

grounding: Illustrates a child told to sit properly, stay quiet and let guests eat first, who misses a favourite dish and notices that home has a public face and a private one.

passage: I'm Rafiq, Reena's neighbour. I'd gone over to borrow her physics notes. Reena, sixteen, had her board exam in two days. Then the bell rang: four relatives, unannounced. Within a minute her mother called, 'Reena, chai banao, and bring the biscuits.' Reena closed her book slowly. Her brother Kunal, a year younger, stayed on the sofa with his game. Nobody called him. I watched Reena carry the tray three times, smile at every aunty and answer questions about her marks. When she came back to her desk, her pen hovered over the same line for ten minutes. Later I heard her ask her mother quietly, 'Can Kunal do the next round?' I don't know what her mother said.

qa.q: When was Reena's board exam?
qa.a: In two days.

qa.q: What does Reena's pen hovering over the same line suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt frustrated and unsettled, unable to focus after being pulled from study while her brother was left alone.

qa.q: What would be a fairer way to handle the surprise guests?
qa.a: Share the serving between Reena and Kunal, or let Kunal take this round since Reena had an exam, while still welcoming the guests warmly.

qa.q: How might Kunal see the evening, and what would change if he were called too?
qa.a: Kunal may not notice the unfairness since nobody asked him; if he were called, he would learn hosting is everyone's job and Reena would get time to study.

grounding: Shows a teenage daughter pulled from exam study to serve tea to unexpected relatives while her brother is left alone, raising the question of fairness in who serves guests.

passage:
Tuesday: Nazia, fifteen, is halfway through a chemistry worksheet when Ammi's cousins arrive without warning. 'Nazia, tea and pakoras, jaldi!' Her brother Faiz, fourteen, keeps watching the cricket. Nazia fries pakoras for an hour. The worksheet stays blank.
Wednesday: In the library, Nazia tells her classmate Anirban, 'I love having guests. I just hate that it's always me.' Anirban asks, 'Have you told your Ammi that?'
Friday: More guests. This time Nazia says quietly, 'Ammi, I have a test tomorrow. Can Faiz make the tea today?' Ammi pauses, then calls, 'Faiz! Kitchen.' Faiz groans, but goes. Nazia serves the plates with a smile, then returns to her books.

qa.q: What was Nazia working on when the guests arrived on Tuesday?
qa.a: A chemistry worksheet.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she told Anirban, 'I just hate that it's always me'?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and resentful about the unfairness, even though she still enjoys having guests.

qa.q: What made Friday go better?
qa.a: Nazia asked Ammi calmly with a clear reason, and Ammi shared the job by calling Faiz, so hosting stayed warm but fairer.

qa.q: How might Faiz see being called into the kitchen?
qa.a: Faiz may feel annoyed at first, but it shows him that serving guests is his job too, not only his sister's.

grounding: Illustrates a teenage daughter repeatedly pulled from study to serve unexpected guests while her brother is left alone, and a fairer sharing of hosting once she speaks up.

passage:
Dear Francis,
You asked why I've gone quiet for two weeks. Ma's cousin, Bablu Mama, arrived 'for two days' to see a doctor in Kolkata. That was eleven days ago. I smile, I give up my bed, I sleep on the sitting-room divan, and every morning I wonder: how long? Ma cooks three meals a day for him and says nothing, because in our house you never ask a guest when he's leaving.
Yesterday I finally sat with him over tea and said, 'Mama, my exams start Monday. Could we plan your dates so I have my room back by then?' He laughed, embarrassed, and said Saturday. Then he offered to take Ma to the market. Maybe asking was kinder than sulking.
Anirban

qa.q: How long has Bablu Mama been staying?
qa.a: Eleven days.

qa.q: What has Anirban been feeling while sleeping on the divan each night?
qa.a: Anirban has felt tired and quietly resentful, smiling on the outside while wondering how long the stay would last.

qa.q: What made Anirban's talk with Bablu Mama work?
qa.a: Anirban spoke privately over tea, gave a real reason and asked to plan the dates together, which was honest without being rude.

qa.q: How might Bablu Mama have felt when Anirban raised the dates?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed at first, but perhaps also relieved to have a plan, and he answered by offering to help Ma.

grounding: Shows a host who smiles while wondering how long a relative will stay, and finds that a gentle, honest talk about timing protects both hospitality and the relationship.

passage: 'You know my cousin Dorjee, from Kalimpong?' Tenzin asks Maria as they walk to class. 'He dropped in three Sundays ago. No call, just a bag and a big smile. Our rule at home is, a guest is a guest. So I rolled out my mattress, cooked thukpa, lent him my laptop. Every night I lay awake thinking, is it one more week? Two? I couldn't just ask. It felt so rude. Then Ama-la did something clever. At dinner she asked him, very sweetly, "Dorjee, when does your college term start? We want to pack you some dried cheese." He told us: Thursday. Nobody was hurt, and I finally slept.'

qa.q: What did Tenzin cook for Dorjee?
qa.a: Thukpa.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling while lying awake each night?
qa.a: Tenzin felt anxious and stuck, wanting to know how long Dorjee would stay but worried that asking would seem rude.

qa.q: Why did Ama-la's question work well?
qa.a: It asked about timing warmly and came with a kind offer, so Dorjee could share his plans without feeling pushed out.

qa.q: How might Dorjee have felt when asked about his college term?
qa.a: Dorjee probably felt cared for rather than unwelcome, since the question came with an offer of food for the journey.

grounding: Illustrates a host who keeps smiling while privately wondering how long an unannounced relative will stay, and a gentle question about timing that protects both hospitality and the relationship.

passage:
When my son's college friend Omkar came to stay a night with us in Ludhiana, I expected the usual: a boy who sleeps till noon and leaves wet towels. Instead he arrived with a small box of Kolhapuri chivda from his mother. After dinner he rolled up his sleeves and asked where the dishes went. I told him to sit; he dried them anyway. Next morning he made his bed, thanked my husband for the lift, and left before lunch, saying, 'Aunty, you must be tired, you cooked so much.' I was. I can't say what went on in his head, but I'd have that boy back any day.
Baljeet

qa.q: What did Omkar bring from his mother?
qa.a: A small box of Kolhapuri chivda.

qa.q: What did Baljeet feel about Omkar's visit?
qa.a: Baljeet felt pleasantly surprised and grateful, touched that he noticed how tiring the cooking had been.

qa.q: Which of Omkar's actions made him a good guest?
qa.a: Bringing a small gift, drying the dishes, making his bed, thanking the hosts and leaving before they grew tired.

qa.q: Why might Omkar have chosen to leave before lunch?
qa.a: He likely sensed that hosting was tiring and wanted to leave while everyone still felt glad, though Baljeet can only guess his thoughts.

grounding: Shows a young adult guest who brings a small gift, helps in the kitchen and leaves before the host is tired, as seen by the host.

passage:
Friday: Before her trip to her college friend Tushar's home in Nashik, Farida, twenty-one, hunts for a gift she can afford and settles on a jar of her Nani's mango pickle.
Saturday: At Tushar's house she hands the jar to his Aai, then follows her into the kitchen. 'Let me cut the onions, at least.' Aai protests, then hands over the knife, laughing. After dinner Farida notices Aai's slow steps and says goodnight early instead of starting another round of cards.
Sunday: She leaves after breakfast, as planned. That evening Tushar forwards a voice note from Aai: 'Tell Farida she's welcome any time. Such a thoughtful girl.'

qa.q: What gift did Farida bring?
qa.a: A jar of her Nani's mango pickle.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when she noticed Aai's slow steps?
qa.a: She felt considerate and a bit concerned, sensing Aai was tired and wanting to let her rest.

qa.q: Which of Farida's choices made her a good guest?
qa.a: A small gift, help in the kitchen, noticing tiredness and saying goodnight early, and leaving when planned.

qa.q: How did Aai experience Farida's visit?
qa.a: Aai felt respected and pleased, calling Farida thoughtful and welcoming her back any time.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult guest who brings a small gift, helps in the kitchen and leaves before the host is tired, showing that being a good guest is a skill.

passage:
Arnab's salary was late again, and Vidya's parents were arriving on Sunday for their first visit to the one-room flat. Arnab had already booked a caterer and bought new curtains and a dinner set on the credit card, telling himself, 'They can't think we're struggling.' On Saturday night the card was declined at the sweet shop. He stood at the counter, face hot.
At home Vidya found the bills on the table. 'Arnab, Baba grew up eating khichuri on a mat. He's coming to see us, not our curtains.' They cancelled the caterer. On Sunday Vidya made khichuri and begun bhaja, and Arnab served it on their old plates. Her father asked for seconds and told stories till midnight.

qa.q: What did Vidya make on Sunday?
qa.a: Khichuri and begun bhaja.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when the card was declined?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and panicked, his face hot, afraid of looking poor in front of Vidya's parents.

qa.q: What went wrong with Arnab's plan, and what helped fix it?
qa.a: He spent beyond what they had to impress the guests; an honest talk with Vidya and a simple home-cooked meal eased the strain.

qa.q: How might Vidya's father have seen the simple Sunday dinner?
qa.a: He seemed truly happy and at home, asking for seconds and telling stories, showing the warmth mattered more than the display.

grounding: Shows a host who spends beyond his means out of fear of looking poor, and discovers that a warm, simple welcome is still real hospitality.

passage:
Tanuja had been planning the reunion lunch in her small Dadar flat for a month. Her old school friends were managers and designers now; she was still a junior clerk. So she bought paneer, prawns, fancy chocolates and a new tablecloth, borrowing from her sister to cover it. On the morning of the lunch she stood in the kitchen counting what was left for the month, and her stomach knotted.
Ritu arrived early and found her staring at the prawns. 'Tanu, what's wrong?' Out it all came. Ritu hugged her. 'We came for you and your aai's poha, silly. Remember school tiffins?'
That afternoon everyone laughed over poha and prawns alike, and nobody mentioned the tablecloth.

qa.q: What was Tanuja's job?
qa.a: A junior clerk.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling as she counted what was left for the month?
qa.a: She felt anxious and ashamed, worried about the money she had borrowed and spent so as not to look poorer than her friends.

qa.q: What could Tanuja keep in mind for the next get-together?
qa.a: That a warm, simple meal like her aai's poha is real hospitality; her friends came to see her, not an expensive spread.

qa.q: How did Ritu see Tanuja's worry?
qa.a: Ritu saw it with affection, reminding Tanuja that the friends came for her and for simple poha, not for show.

grounding: Illustrates a host who borrows and overspends to impress visitors out of fear of looking poor, and learns from a friend that a simple, warm welcome is enough.

passage: I'm Shalini, and I shared a flat in Frankfurt with Rehana last winter. The first time our German neighbour, Frau Keller, offered her cake, Rehana smiled and said, 'No, no, thank you,' the way we do at home, waiting for the second offer. It never came. Frau Keller simply nodded and put the cake away. Rehana's face fell a little. Later, when Rehana invited Frau Keller for biryani, she insisted three times; Frau Keller looked uneasy and took a tiny spoonful. The next time, I watched Rehana say, 'Yes, please, just a small piece,' and Frau Keller beamed. I think they both learnt something, though neither said so.

qa.q: What did Frau Keller offer Rehana the first time?
qa.a: Cake.

qa.q: What does Shalini's last line suggest Shalini felt watching the two neighbours?
qa.a: Shalini felt amused and fond, watching both of them slowly and quietly learn each other's rules.

qa.q: What could Rehana and Frau Keller each do to avoid such awkward moments?
qa.a: Learn the local rule: Rehana can accept directly, and Frau Keller can know that an Indian host may insist out of warmth, not pressure.

qa.q: How did Rehana seem to feel when the second offer never came?
qa.a: Rehana seemed disappointed and a little embarrassed, since at home a first 'no' is only politeness.

grounding: Shows a young person observing that one culture expects the host to insist and the guest to refuse, while another takes a first no as final, and how learning the local rule eases awkwardness.

passage:
Monday: At her colleague Raghav's home in Delhi, Lalremsiami, twenty-four, politely declines a third helping of rajma. Raghav's mother puts two more spoonfuls on her plate anyway. In Lalremsiami's family in Aizawl, a clear no is taken as final, so she eats slowly and says nothing.
Wednesday: Over office tea she asks Raghav about it. He laughs. 'In our house the first no means maybe, and the second means please insist. Mummy thought you were being shy.'
Saturday: At the next visit, when Raghav's mother offers more, Lalremsiami smiles and says, 'Aunty, I'm truly full. Your rajma is too good.' His mother laughs and, for once, puts the ladle down.

qa.q: What dish was Lalremsiami offered more of?
qa.a: Rajma.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling as she ate the extra spoonfuls slowly?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and confused, too polite to protest but unsure why her clear no had been ignored.

qa.q: What helped Lalremsiami handle the next offer?
qa.a: Asking Raghav about the custom, then declining warmly and praising the food, so Aunty could hear the no as real.

qa.q: How had Raghav's mother seen Lalremsiami's refusals?
qa.a: She thought Lalremsiami was being shy, since in her house a guest's first refusals invite the host to insist.

grounding: Illustrates a young person noticing that one family expects the host to insist past a guest's refusals while her own takes a first no as final, and learning the local rule to avoid awkwardness.

passage:
From the next mat at the wedding lunch, I watched two-year-old Kunal grab a fistful of rice from his mother's leaf, squash it, and push it toward my mouth. I took it; he looked thrilled. Then he reached for a piece of my papad and a pinch of his sister's sweet, as if every plate were his. He gave just as freely, offering a soggy bite to the cat. He seemed to think eating was something everyone did together.
Santosh

qa.q: What did Kunal offer the cat?
qa.a: A soggy bite.

qa.q: What does Kunal's thrilled look suggest he felt when Santosh took the rice?
qa.a: He felt delighted and proud, happy that his offer of food was accepted, as if sharing were a game of closeness.

qa.q: How could adults respond to Kunal's sharing at this age?
qa.a: Enjoy his generosity and accept small offers, while gently steering what goes to the cat, without scolding him for mixing plates.

qa.q: How might Kunal's mother feel watching him feed Santosh?
qa.a: She may feel amused and a bit embarrassed, but also warmed by how freely he shares.

grounding: Shows a toddler who grabs food, feeds others from his own hand and takes bites from everyone's plate, treating food as a way of being close.

passage:
Monday: Avni, twenty months, sits on Mumma Tanuja's lap, grabs a fistful of dal-rice from her plate, and pushes a squashed ball into Mumma's mouth. Mumma chews, laughing.
Wednesday: At lunch, Avni waddles from Nani's plate to Nanu's to her cousin's, taking a bite from each and offering her own in return, sticky fingers and all.
Sunday: At the park picnic, Avni holds out a half-eaten banana to a stranger's toddler. The other child takes a bite. Both beam.

qa.q: What did Avni offer the stranger's toddler at the picnic?
qa.a: A half-eaten banana.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling as she went from plate to plate at Wednesday's lunch?
qa.a: She felt happy and close to everyone, treating each plate as shared and giving her own food back just as gladly.

qa.q: What could Mumma Tanuja keep in mind at picnics with other children?
qa.a: Enjoy Avni's sharing while quietly checking with the other parent before food is passed along.

qa.q: What is it like for Mumma Tanuja when Avni pushes food into her mouth?
qa.a: Mumma finds it funny and sweet, laughing as she chews, happy to be fed by her little one.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler who feeds others from her own hand and expects bites from everyone's plate, with sharing food as bonding and no idea yet of clean or unclean.

passage:
In their Bengaluru flat, five-year-old Usha took a bite of banana and ran to put the rest on the little puja shelf for Ganesha. Ajji Nirmala caught her wrist gently. 'Not that one, kanda. Something you've bitten is jootha. God gets the first, fresh piece.'
Usha frowned. 'But I didn't bite much.'
Ajji smiled and gave her a whole banana to offer. At dinner, when Usha reached for Appa's steel tumbler, she stopped herself. 'Jootha,' she announced, and fetched her own. She still wasn't sure why. She only knew some things sat on one side of an invisible line.

qa.q: What did Ajji give Usha to offer?
qa.a: A whole banana.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she frowned and said, 'But I didn't bite much'?
qa.a: She felt confused and a little disappointed, not understanding why her bitten banana wasn't good enough.

qa.q: How could Ajji help Usha understand the rule, not just follow it?
qa.a: Explain simply, when Usha asks, that offering the first, fresh piece is a way of showing care and respect, and answer her questions kindly.

qa.q: How might Ajji Nirmala feel seeing Usha fetch her own tumbler?
qa.a: Ajji may feel pleased and a little amused that Usha is already following the family custom on her own.

grounding: Shows a young child told not to offer bitten food at the shrine or drink from another's glass, who follows the jootha rule before understanding it.

passage:
'Zubin, don't drink from Manoj's glass, dikra. That's eththu.'
'What's eththu, Mamma?'
'Jootha. Once someone's lips touch it, it's theirs.'
'But Manoj is my best friend.'
'Even best friends get their own glass. Here.'
Manoj grinned. 'My Dadi says the same thing! Jootha!'
'Then why do you share your chocolate with me?'
'Because I break it first, silly.'
Zubin thought hard, then carefully broke his biscuit in two before offering half. 'Not eththu,' he told Mamma proudly.
'Very good,' Mamma said, trying not to laugh.

qa.q: What did Zubin break in two before offering it?
qa.a: His biscuit.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when he said 'Not eththu' to Mamma?
qa.a: He felt proud and pleased, happy to have followed the new rule correctly even without fully understanding it.

qa.q: How did Mamma handle Zubin's question in a helpful way?
qa.a: She gave a simple reason, offered his own glass, and praised his effort without mocking how literally he took the rule.

qa.q: How might Manoj feel hearing that Zubin's family has the same rule as his Dadi?
qa.a: Manoj seems happy and excited to find something in common, shouting 'Jootha!' with a grin.

grounding: Illustrates a young child learning not to drink from another's glass and to offer unbitten food, following the rule before understanding it.

passage: I'm Sudha. Last Saturday I went to Hemant's house for his birthday. At the door his mother asked if I had eggs in my tiffin, because their kitchen has no eggs at all. Inside I saw two sets of steel plates, and Hemant's Dadi ate only from her own. I wanted to giggle, because at our house Papa makes egg curry every Sunday. But I remembered how Anjali laughed at my fish smell last year and how bad it felt. So I asked Hemant, 'Why two sets?' He said, 'Dadi's are for her fasting days.' I said, 'Oh. We have a special plate for Nani too.' He looked relieved.

qa.q: Why does Hemant's Dadi have her own plates?
qa.a: Dadi's are for her fasting days.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling on wanting to giggle, and what stopped it?
qa.a: Sudha felt amused and curious, but remembered how hurt and embarrassed Anjali's laughing at the fish smell had made Sudha feel.

qa.q: What could another child learn from how Sudha asked about the plates?
qa.a: To ask kindly and share something similar from home instead of laughing, which keeps the friendship easy.

qa.q: How did Hemant seem to feel when Sudha asked kindly?
qa.a: Hemant seemed relieved, perhaps because he expected teasing and was met with interest instead.

grounding: Shows a child noticing a friend's home has different kitchen rules, such as no eggs and separate plates, and choosing to ask kindly rather than mock.

passage:
Thursday: At Ojas's house for a school project, Kashish, nine, notices a small shelf of blue plates kept apart from the steel ones. Ojas's Aai serves Kashish on steel. Why blue? Kashish wonders, but says nothing.
Saturday: Kashish asks Ma at home. Ma says, 'Why not ask Ojas? Kindly, like you're curious, not like it's weird.'
Monday: At recess Kashish asks, 'Ojas, what are the blue plates for?' Ojas shrugs. 'For chicken. Aaji doesn't eat it, so we keep hers separate.' Kashish nods. 'We don't eat onion in Navratri, so Ma keeps a separate pan too.' Ojas grins. 'Everyone has a weird pan.'

qa.q: What are the blue plates for?
qa.a: For chicken.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling on Thursday on seeing the blue plates?
qa.a: Kashish felt curious and a little unsure, wondering about the plates but too shy to ask right away.

qa.q: Which part of Ma's advice made the Monday talk go well?
qa.a: Asking out of curiosity, not as if the custom were strange, so Ojas could explain without feeling mocked.

qa.q: How does Ojas seem to feel about explaining the blue plates?
qa.a: Ojas seems relaxed and at ease, even joking that everyone has a weird pan, because Kashish asked kindly.

grounding: Illustrates a child who notices a friend's home keeps separate plates, and learns to ask kindly out of curiosity rather than mock, keeping the friendship open.

passage:
'Ugh, what's that smell?' someone at the next table said.
Rafiq snapped his tiffin shut. 'Nothing.'
Siddharth leaned over. 'Is that your Ammi's fish curry? The one from the Eid party?'
'It stinks. Everyone's looking.'
'Everyone's jealous. Give me one piece, please. I've got boring cheese sandwiches again.'
'You actually like it?'
'Bro, I dreamed about it.'
Rafiq opened the tiffin slowly. Siddharth took a piece and closed his eyes. 'Your Ammi is a genius.'
Two others drifted over. 'Can we try?'
Rafiq split the pieces, ears red, but smiling now. 'Tomorrow I'll ask her to pack extra.'

qa.q: What was in Rafiq's tiffin?
qa.a: His Ammi's fish curry.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he snapped the tiffin shut?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and ashamed, worried that everyone was looking at his strong-smelling lunch.

qa.q: How did Siddharth turn the moment around?
qa.a: He praised the dish sincerely and asked to share it, showing the others that home food is something to enjoy, not mock.

qa.q: How might Rafiq's Ammi feel when asked to pack extra tomorrow?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and happy that her cooking is loved by Rafiq's friends.

grounding: Shows a teenager embarrassed by a strong-smelling home lunch whose shame turns to pride when a friend asks to share it.

passage:
In Class 8 I started telling Amma I'd eat in the canteen. The truth was, I was hiding my ragi mudde. The first day I opened it, Kishore said it looked like a grey cricket ball, and three people laughed. I ate it alone in the corridor for a week.
Then, this year, our teacher asked everyone to bring a traditional dish. I almost brought pasta. But I took ragi mudde with Amma's soppu saaru, and I explained how my Ajji ate it every day in the fields. Kishore tried it first. He asked for the recipe. I'm still a little shy about how it looks. But now I'm proud too.
Leela

qa.q: What did Kishore say the ragi mudde looked like?
qa.a: A grey cricket ball.

qa.q: How does Leela feel about the ragi mudde now?
qa.a: Leela feels proud of it now, though still a little shy about how it looks.

qa.q: What helped Leela move from hiding the dish to sharing it?
qa.a: The traditional-dish project gave a chance to explain its story, and a classmate trying it respectfully turned shame into pride.

qa.q: How might Kishore have felt when he tried it and asked for the recipe?
qa.a: Kishore probably felt curious and maybe a bit sorry for the old joke, and asking for the recipe showed real respect.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who once hid a home dish out of embarrassment after peers mocked it, and grows proud of it when classmates respond with interest.
